game-osint-profile.intro: Scattered public data. What does it tell you?

challenges.q: A job advert asks for Kubernetes, Terraform and AWS EKS experience. What have you learned?
a: The cloud stack and likely the orchestration platform in use
challenges.why: Recruitment posts describe the technology stack in detail.

challenges.q: certificate transparency logs show admin-staging.internal.example.com. What does this give you?
a: A hostname that may never have appeared in public DNS
challenges.why: CT logs are public by design and leak internal-sounding hostnames.

challenges.q: A company PDF has Author: jsmith and Producer: Microsoft Word 2010. What have you learned?
a: A likely username and an end of life software version
challenges.why: Document metadata names authors and the software that made it.

challenges.q: A GitHub repository has an old commit containing AWS credentials. Is this in scope of a finding?
a: Yes, exposed credentials in public repos are a serious finding
challenges.why: Publicly exposed credentials are a real, and common, exposure.

challenges.q: An employee posts a photo from the office with a badge visible. What is the OSINT value?
a: Badge design and physical access details, useful for social engineering
challenges.why: Physical and social details support other attack paths.

challenges.q: Shodan shows port 3389 open on the company perimeter. What is the concern?
a: RDP exposed to the internet is a primary ransomware entry point
challenges.why: Internet-facing RDP is a leading cause of ransomware incidents.

challenges.q: A conference talk by their lead engineer describes their architecture in detail. This is
a: Valuable passive intelligence about internal design
challenges.why: Public technical talks frequently describe internals.

challenges.q: Whois shows a registration email of an unrelated personal address. What might this indicate?
a: Registration by an individual, possibly the original tech contact, useful for phishing or social engineering
challenges.why: Historical registration data often names the original technical contact.

game-vhost-hunt.intro: Which Host header reveals the hidden site?

challenges.q: The default site returns a generic placeholder. Fuzzing Host headers, you see a different page for one value. Give the standard first guess.
The main site is example.com. Give a likely admin vhost name.
Give a likely internal or development vhost name for example.com.
A different response appears when the Host header has no valid virtual host. What does that tell you?
challenges.hint: Difference in response means routing exists

challenges.q: Which status code most strongly suggests a vhost exists but is forbidden?
You must enumerate many vhost names quickly. What kind of file drives the fuzzing?

game-attack-surface.intro: Rank the findings by real-world risk. Most severe first.

challenges.q: Order these by risk, highest first.
items: Unauthenticated RCE on an internet-facing service
SQL injection on a public login form
Stored XSS in an authenticated admin panel
Verbose error messages revealing the framework
challenges.why: Un authenticated remote code execution on the perimeter is the worst case: no credentials, no user interaction, full control.

challenges.q: Order these by risk, highest first.
items: Hardcoded cloud credentials in a public repository
Weak password policy with no lockout
Missing security headers
Server banner disclosure
challenges.why: Live credentials in public code grant immediate access, whereas the others raise risk without granting it.

challenges.q: Order these by risk, highest first.
items: Exposed Docker socket reachable from the internet
Open SMB with guest access
Public S3 bucket listing internal documents
Unpatched CMS with a public exploit but no known usage
challenges.why: The Docker socket is immediate host compromise; guest SMB and public buckets follow; an unconfirmed exploit is lowest.

challenges.q: Order the reconnaissance steps from least to most likely to touch the target.
items: Reading certificate transparency logs
Querying passive DNS history
Resolving a wordlist of subdomains
Port scanning with service detection
challenges.why: CT and passive DNS use third parties; resolution touches DNS; scanning makes direct contact.

challenges.q: Order the response priority in the first hour of an incident.
items: Determine scope and whether the attack is ongoing
Contain affected systems without destroying evidence
Eradicate the persistence mechanism
Notify stakeholders and regulators as required
challenges.why: Scope first, then contain, then remove persistence, then communicate. Communicating before you know scope produces inaccurate statements.
